text: The rate limiter sits in front of every route under /api/v2 and uses a token bucket per API key. Each key gets a bucket of 600 tokens that refills at 10 tokens per second, so a client can burst briefly but cannot sustain more than 600 requests per minute. Limits are configured in config/ratelimit.yaml. The buckets live in Redis, which means the limit is shared across all application replicas, but it also means a Redis outage will cause the limiter to fail open by default. Set RATELIMIT_FAIL_CLOSED=true if you would rather reject requests during an outage. Responses that exceed the limit return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds. Internal service-to-service calls authenticated with a mesh certificate bypass the limiter entirely. If you add a new route group, register it in routes/index.ts so it inherits the middleware. Routes mounted directly on the app object are not rate limited.

If the migration job fails on 0042_split_users with the error relation users_v2 already exists, the previous run got partway through and left the table behind. The migration is not idempotent because the CREATE TABLE statement has no IF NOT EXISTS guard. Check the schema_migrations table first. If 0042 is not listed there, it is safe to drop users_v2 manually, since the copy step is repeated from scratch on the next run. Do not drop it if any rows were written to it after the failed run started, because those rows would be lost. Ask in the data-platform channel before touching production. Staging can be reset with make db-reset, which reruns every migration from zero. A proper fix that adds the IF NOT EXISTS guard is tracked in DP-881.

List endpoints use cursor-based pagination rather than page numbers. Each response includes a next_cursor field when more results exist. Pass that value back as the cursor query parameter to fetch the following page. When next_cursor is null, you have reached the end. The page size defaults to 50 and can be raised to a maximum of 200 with the limit parameter. Cursors are opaque strings and should not be parsed or constructed by clients. They expire after 24 hours. An expired cursor returns 410 Gone, and the client should restart the listing from the beginning. Sorting is fixed to created_at descending for this endpoint, so items created while you are paginating may appear at the top of the list but will not shift the pages you have already read. Example: GET /v2/orders?limit=100 and then GET /v2/orders?limit=100&cursor=eyJpZCI6 using the value from the previous response.

2.7.0 (2026-09-14). Added the bulk export endpoint at POST /v2/exports, which accepts up to 25,000 record IDs and returns a signed download URL valid for one hour. Changed the default timeout for webhook delivery from 5 seconds to 15 seconds after several customers reported false failures on slow endpoints. Deprecated the legacy X-Api-Token header. It still works but logs a warning and will be removed in 3.0. Fixed a bug where timezone offsets were dropped when serializing scheduled_at on the calendar resource. Fixed an issue where the SDK retried non-idempotent POST requests on 502 responses, which could create duplicate invoices. Upgrade notes: no migration is required for 2.7.0. Review the webhook timeout setting if you rely on the old 5 second behavior to detect dead endpoints quickly.

Short answer: your effect runs after every render because you left out the dependency array. Without it, React runs the effect after each commit. Since your effect calls setItems, which triggers another render, you get an infinite loop. Add an empty array if you only want it on mount: useEffect(() => { fetchItems().then(setItems) }, []). If the effect depends on a prop like userId, list it in the array so it re-runs when that value changes. A couple of other things to check. First, if you add fetchItems to the array, make sure it is not redefined inline with new identity on every render, because that will cause the same loop. Wrap it in useCallback or move it outside the component. Second, React 18 StrictMode mounts components twice in development, so you will see the request fire twice locally. That is expected and does not happen in production builds. Hope this helps.

The worker service consumes jobs from the ingest queue and writes normalized records to the warehouse. It is deployed as a separate Kubernetes Deployment from the API, so scaling one does not affect the other. Each worker pod reads from the queue with a prefetch count of 20 and acknowledges messages only after the write commits. If a worker crashes mid-batch, unacknowledged messages are redelivered to another pod, which means the write path must be idempotent. Records are keyed by source_id and upserted, so replays are safe. Concurrency is controlled by the WORKER_CONCURRENCY environment variable, which defaults to 4 per pod. Increasing it beyond 8 is not recommended because the warehouse connection pool is capped at 32 connections per pod. Logs are emitted as JSON to stdout and shipped to the central logging stack. Metrics are exposed on port 9100 at /metrics. The most useful dashboard is ingest-lag, which shows the age of the oldest unacknowledged message.

Install the CLI with npm install -g @acme/cli or with Homebrew using brew install acme/tap/acme. After installation, run acme login to authenticate. The login command opens a browser window for OAuth and stores a refresh token in your OS keychain. On Linux without a keychain daemon it falls back to ~/.config/acme/credentials with file mode 600. If you run the CLI in CI, skip the interactive flow and set ACME_TOKEN as a secret instead. The CLI requires Node.js 18 or later. Running on Node 16 produces a cryptic error about fetch being undefined, so check node --version first. To verify the install, run acme --version and acme whoami. The second command should print your workspace name and role. Shell completions are available for bash, zsh, and fish via acme completion --shell zsh. Add the output to your shell profile or place it in your completions directory. Upgrades are handled by re-running the install command. There is no auto-update.

We use Postgres advisory locks to make sure only one scheduler instance runs each cron job at a time. Each job name is hashed to a 64-bit integer and passed to pg_try_advisory_lock. If the lock is already held, the instance skips the run and logs a debug line. We picked this over Redis-based locks because the database is already a dependency of every job and we did not want to add a new failure mode. The tradeoff is that the lock is tied to a database session, so if the connection drops, the lock is released and another instance may start the job while the first one is still running. To guard against that, every job writes a heartbeat row every 30 seconds and the next instance checks it before starting. This is not perfect, and a job that stalls for longer than the heartbeat window can overlap. We accepted that for now because all current jobs are idempotent. If we ever add a job that is not, revisit this decision and consider a fencing token.

The client retries transient failures automatically. By default it makes up to three retries for responses with status 429, 500, 502, 503, and 504, and for network errors that occur before a response is received. Backoff starts at 500 milliseconds and doubles on each attempt, with full jitter applied. You can change the behavior when constructing the client. Pass maxRetries to set the number of attempts, or pass retryOn to provide a function that receives the error and returns a boolean. Retries are only applied to idempotent methods unless you set idempotencyKey on the request. When you set an idempotency key, the server returns the cached response for repeated requests with the same key within 24 hours. Be careful with payments. If you retry a charge without a key, the customer can be billed twice. The SDK will not warn you about this, so make sure your code sets a key on any non-GET call that creates money movement.

If the local dev server fails with NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID in the browser, the mkcert root certificate has probably expired or was never installed in your system trust store. Run make certs to regenerate the certificates in ./certs. The task also prints the command you need to trust the root CA. On macOS this is sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain certs/rootCA.pem. Restart the browser after installing the root, because some browsers cache the trust decision. Firefox keeps its own trust store and needs the CA imported manually under Settings, Privacy and Security, View Certificates, Authorities. If you still see the error after doing all of this, check that the hostname in your browser matches one of the SANs in certs/localhost.pem. The file lists dev.local and localhost by default. Using 127.0.0.1 directly will fail because it is not in the certificate.

You are in a detached HEAD state, which means HEAD points directly at a commit rather than a branch. This usually happens when you check out a tag, a specific commit hash, or a remote branch without creating a local tracking branch. Any commits you make now are not attached to a branch, so they will be lost when you switch away unless you save them. To keep your work, create a branch at the current position with git switch -c my-fix. If you already switched away and want to get the commits back, run git reflog to find the hash of your last commit, then run git branch recovered-work followed by that hash. The reflog keeps entries for around 90 days by default, so the work is usually recoverable. If you just want to go back to a branch and you made no new commits, git switch main is enough and nothing is lost.

Feature flags that have been at 100 percent rollout for more than 90 days should be removed. The cleanup process has four steps. First, an engineer opens a ticket with the flag name and the date it reached full rollout. Second, the owning team confirms no other service reads the flag by searching the flag registry for the key. Third, the engineer removes the conditional branches and deletes the flag from the config service in a single pull request, so the code and config stay in sync. Fourth, the flag is archived rather than hard deleted, which keeps the audit history. Flags that are still at partial rollout after 90 days must have an owner comment explaining why. Quarterly reports list all stale flags and are posted to the eng-hygiene channel. Please do not leave flags behind after an experiment ends. Stale flags make the codebase harder to reason about, and two incidents this year were caused by a dead branch that was accidentally re-enabled.

2.7.1 (2026-09-22). Patch release. Fixed a crash in the CSV importer when a header row contained trailing whitespace. The importer now trims column names before matching. Fixed an incorrect count in the audit log summary when entries were filtered by actor. Fixed the sort order of the Activity tab, which had been showing oldest entries first on Safari 17 only. Improved error messages for invalid date ranges. The API now names the offending field and the expected format. Internal: upgraded the PDF renderer to 4.2.1 to address a memory leak on documents with more than 500 pages. No API changes. No configuration changes. Customers on self-hosted deployments should restart the application after upgrading so the new renderer loads.

Configuration is read from environment variables at startup. Variables not listed here fall back to the defaults in src/config/defaults.ts. DATABASE_URL is required and must be a Postgres connection string. REDIS_URL is optional. If it is unset, caching is disabled and each request hits the database. LOG_LEVEL accepts debug, info, warn, or error and defaults to info. PORT defaults to 8080. SESSION_TTL_SECONDS controls how long login sessions last and defaults to 86400. FEATURE_NEW_SEARCH enables the search rewrite and defaults to false. In production, do not set LOG_LEVEL to debug, since debug output includes request bodies and can contain personal data. Secrets should not be placed in .env files committed to the repository. Use your secrets manager and inject values at deploy time. The app validates required variables on boot and exits with code 78 if any are missing or malformed. The reason is printed in the logs as a config error with the variable name.

To deploy the worker service, merge to main and wait for the deploy-staging job to finish. Then trigger deploy-prod from the pipeline page. The pipeline runs database migrations as a separate job before rolling the Deployment, so a migration failure will stop the rollout and leave the old pods running. Check the migration job logs if the pipeline shows red at the migrate stage. Rollbacks are done with kubectl rollout undo deployment/worker -n ingest. Rolling back the code does not roll back migrations. If the new version added a column that the old version ignores, that is fine. If the migration dropped something, you will need to restore from backup. Canary releases are not configured for this service. Every deploy goes to all pods at once, with a maxUnavailable of 25 percent. Plan prod deploys outside the 14:00 to 16:00 UTC window, when the batch loads run.

So we hit this on Tuesday. Ran the migrations on staging and 0042_split_users blew up with relation users_v2 already exists. Turns out the previous attempt died halfway through the copy, and the CREATE TABLE has no IF NOT EXISTS, so the second run tripped over the leftover table. I checked schema_migrations and 0042 was not in there, so I dropped users_v2 on staging and reran it. Worked fine. Prod is a different story, obviously we did not drop anything there without asking. Pinged the data platform channel and they said the rows written after the failed run would be gone, so we left it alone and Kaveri wrote a manual recovery. The real fix is DP-881 which adds the guard. Until that lands, if you see this, do not just drop the table on prod. Check for writes first. Also make db-reset is the easy way to get staging back to clean.

ok so the list endpoints dont do page numbers, they do cursors. response gives you next_cursor, you send that back as cursor= and get the next batch. when next_cursor is null thats the end, dont keep looping. default limit is 50, max 200 I think. cursors expire after a day, if you get a 410 just start over from the top, dont try to fix the cursor cause its opaque anyway. also sort is always created_at desc and you cant change it on this one, which is annoying but whatever. new stuff added while you page can show up at the top, it wont mess up pages you already got tho. example GET /v2/orders?limit=100 then the cursor thing. hope that helps, lmk if the docs are confusing and ill fix them.

Upgrading to Node 20.11.1 broke our build on the arm64 CI runners. The error was: Error: Cannot find module @swc/core-linux-arm64-gnu, with the dependency tree showing @swc/core 1.3.82 as the parent. The cause is that npm did not install the optional native binary, because the lockfile was generated on an x64 machine and pinned only the x64 variant. The fix is to regenerate the lockfile on an arm64 host, or run npm install --force once locally to pull the platform binaries, then commit the result. We bumped @swc/core to 1.4.2 in the meantime, which lists all the platform variants in its optional dependencies, and that fixed it. If you see the same error on a different package, check whether it has platform specific optionalDependencies. Pinning Node 20.11.0 also avoids the problem, but we did not want to hold back security patches.

The client do automatic retry for some errors. By default it retry up to three times for status 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504, and also for network error before response come back. Wait time start at 500 milliseconds and it double every attempt, with random jitter added. For changing this, you can set maxRetries when you create the client to change the number of tries. There is also retryOn option, you give a function that get the error and return true or false. Important: retry only work for idempotent method unless you give idempotencyKey in the request. With idempotencyKey, server will return the same saved response for same key in 24 hours. For payment, please be careful. If you retry a charge without key, customer can get charged two times. SDK does not warn you about this, so always set a key for any POST that move money.

Flag cleanup. so anything at 100% for 90+ days, remove it. steps: 1) ticket w/ flag name + date it hit full rollout 2) owner checks nobody else reads the key (search flag registry) 3) one PR removes the branches AND deletes the flag from config. same PR, otherwise code and config drift apart. 4) archive, dont hard delete, we need the audit trail. Partial rollout flags older than 90 days need an owner comment saying why theyre still around. Quarterly list goes to the eng-hygiene channel. Please dont leave experiment flags lying around after the test ends. We had two incidents where a dead branch got turned back on because someone flipped a stale flag. Not fun. Questions to Dana or just ask in the channel.

We got bitten by the worker re-processing batches last month. A pod got OOM killed mid-batch, the messages were never acked so they went back on the queue, and another pod wrote them again. Because the write was a plain INSERT we ended up with around 3k duplicate rows in the warehouse, and the revenue dashboard was off for a day. Now the upsert keys on source_id so replays are harmless. Lesson for anyone adding a consumer: assume every message can arrive twice. Also the prefetch was set to 200, which made it worse because a crashed pod held 200 unacked messages. Dropped it to 20. WORKER_CONCURRENCY default is still 4 per pod. Dont push it past 8 unless you also raise the warehouse pool, which is capped at 32 per pod. The ingest-lag dashboard is the one to watch.

2.7.0 (2026-09-14). New: bulk export at POST /v2/exports, takes up to 25000 IDs and gives back a signed URL good for one hour. Webhook delivery timeout went from 5s to 15s, because a few customers were getting false failures on slow endpoints. Heads up, X-Api-Token is deprecated. It still works, logs a warning, and goes away in 3.0. Fixed: timezone offsets were getting dropped when scheduled_at was serialized on calendar resources. Fixed: SDK was retrying POSTs on 502, which could double-create invoices. No migrations needed for this one. If you were depending on the old 5 second timeout to catch dead endpoints quickly, you will want to look at your own timeout handling now.

Heads up on the advisory locks in the scheduler. Each job name gets hashed to a 64 bit int and we call pg_try_advisory_lock on it. If the lock is taken, the instance just skips the run and logs at debug. We went with this instead of Redis locks because every job already depends on the DB, so no new failure mode to worry about. Downside: the lock lives on the DB session, so if the connection drops, the lock goes away and another instance can start the job while the first one still runs. We added a heartbeat row every 30s and the next instance checks it before starting, which covers most cases but not all. A job that stalls longer than the heartbeat window can overlap. Fine for now since all current jobs are idempotent. Any new job that isnt idempotent means we need to revisit this and probably use a fencing token.

Local certs keep breaking for me so writing this down. If the dev server gives NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID, the mkcert root is either expired or never made it into the system trust store. I ran make certs which regenerates everything in ./certs and prints the trust command. On my mac that was sudo security add-trusted-cert with the rootCA.pem path. Then I had to fully restart Chrome, it kept the old decision cached. Firefox has its own store, so I imported the CA by hand under Settings, Privacy and Security, View Certificates, Authorities. Still failing for me once because I was going to 127.0.0.1 directly, which is not a SAN in the cert. Use localhost or dev.local instead.

The Great Wall of China is the only human made structure visible from space with the naked eye, and this shows how impressive human construction can be. Built over many centuries by different dynasties, the wall stretches for thousands of miles across mountains and deserts, and its scale reflects the huge labor and organization needed to build it. Some people think the wall was built mainly to keep out invaders, but it was also used to control trade, collect taxes, and send messages quickly using signal towers. The wall also shows the cost of defense. Millions of workers were involved, many of them conscripts who died during construction. Today it is a major tourist site and a symbol of Chinese history. Its legacy raises a question about whether big projects are worth the human cost, and historians still debate how much the wall actually stopped attacks. In my view, the wall is best understood as a record of a society's ambitions and its limits.

Many high schools start before 8 a.m., even though research on adolescent sleep is fairly consistent. Teenagers' circadian rhythms shift later during puberty, and most do not get the eight to ten hours of sleep recommended by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. Starting school later, around 8:30 or 9 a.m., would give students more rest and, by extension, better attention in class. Critics argue that later start times would disrupt bus schedules and after-school jobs, and some districts that tried it did face real logistical costs. These costs are mostly administrative, and administrative problems can be solved with planning. A district can stagger bus routes or move elementary schools to earlier times. The health and academic benefits reach every student, while the inconvenience falls mostly on adults who can adjust their schedules. A later start is a small policy change with a large payoff, and the evidence supports making it.

Governments that want to restrict social media for children under 16 have a legitimate concern. Platforms are designed around engagement, and teenagers are especially vulnerable to notifications, comparison, and the constant pull of infinite feeds. Several studies have linked heavy use to worse sleep and higher rates of anxiety among adolescents, although the size and direction of these effects remain debated. A ban is a blunt tool, and critics are right that it may push young people toward platforms that are less regulated, and that it may cut off support communities for isolated kids. Still, relying on voluntary parental controls has not worked well, because most controls are hard to use and easy to bypass. A better approach combines an age floor with rules that require platforms to turn off addictive design features for minors, such as autoplay and overnight notifications. This targets the mechanism rather than the access itself, and it would protect children without treating every online interaction as harmful.

Homework is often defended as a way to reinforce what students learn in class, yet the evidence for its benefits depends heavily on age. For elementary students, research suggests that homework has little measurable effect on achievement, and it can make children resent learning. For high school students, the picture is more positive, particularly when assignments are focused and checked. The problem is that many teachers assign work without thinking about how long it will take, and students in demanding schools can end up with hours of work each night. This leaves less time for sleep, family, and reading for pleasure, all of which matter for development. I think schools should limit homework for younger children to short reading tasks and make high school assignments shorter but more deliberate. Quality should count for more than volume. Districts that have already adopted these limits have not reported drops in test scores, which suggests that the old model was not doing as much as its supporters assumed.

Remote work is often described as a productivity boost, but the reality is more complicated. Employees save commuting time and can work during the hours when they focus best, and many report fewer interruptions from colleagues. Those gains are real, especially for people with heavy individual tasks such as writing code or analysing data. However, remote work also weakens the informal communication that builds trust and spreads knowledge across a team. New hires struggle to learn how things are done when they cannot watch experienced colleagues. Managers may find it harder to recognize quiet contributions, and careers can stall for people who are not visible. The best arrangement is probably hybrid, with a few shared days each week for planning, mentoring, and collaborative work, and independent days for deep focus. Companies that treat remote work as a complete replacement for the office tend to lose the things that the office did well, while companies that reject it entirely lose talent. A balanced model keeps the benefits of both.

Standardized tests are frequently criticized as a narrow measure of learning, and that criticism has merit. A single exam taken on one morning can be affected by illness, stress, or a bad night's sleep, and it rewards test-taking strategies that do not always reflect real understanding. Teachers also feel pressure to narrow their lessons to what will be tested. Nevertheless, standardized tests serve a purpose that other measures do not. They allow parents and policymakers to compare schools on a common scale, and they can reveal gaps that would otherwise stay hidden, particularly for students from low-income families whose schools may have lower expectations. Without a shared benchmark, a district can report high grades while its students struggle with basic reading. The answer is not to abandon testing but to design better tests. Exams that include open-ended questions, performance tasks, and multiple measures across the school year would give a fuller picture. Standardized tests should remain part of education, but they should be one piece of a broader system of evidence.

Zoos are sometimes defended as centers of conservation, and a few certainly are. Accredited zoos run breeding programs for endangered species such as the California condor and the black-footed ferret, and they fund field work that protects habitats. These contributions matter. Yet most zoo animals are not part of these programs, and the average zoo keeps many species that have no conservation role at all. Animals such as elephants and large carnivores often live in enclosures that are far smaller than the territory they would cover in the wild, and studies of stereotypic behavior, such as pacing and swaying, suggest that many suffer from boredom or stress. Visitors may learn something from seeing an animal in person, but the educational value of a zoo can often be matched by high quality video and by visits to wildlife reserves. I do not think zoos should disappear entirely. However, they should be held to strict standards, with fewer species, larger habitats, and a clear conservation purpose. A zoo that cannot meet those standards should not exist.

Nuclear power is one of the few sources of electricity that produces almost no carbon emissions while providing steady output day and night. For a country trying to decarbonize its grid, that reliability matters, because wind and solar depend on weather and storage technology is still expensive at large scale. France generates most of its electricity from nuclear plants and has among the lowest per capita carbon emissions in Europe. Critics raise valid concerns about radioactive waste, construction delays, and cost overruns, which have plagued projects in the United States and Europe. Still, these problems are largely the result of policy and project management, not an inherent flaw in the technology. Standardized reactor designs, streamlined licensing, and experienced construction crews could reduce both cost and delay. Waste is a manageable engineering problem, since the volume of spent fuel is small compared with the emissions it prevents. A serious climate plan should include nuclear power alongside renewables, not treat it as a rival that must be excluded.

Supporters of school uniforms argue that they reduce peer pressure, cut down on bullying related to clothing, and save families money on clothes. Those points deserve consideration. When every student wears the same outfit, differences in wealth become less visible, and parents do not have to buy expensive brands to avoid being judged. Some schools that adopted uniforms reported improvements in attendance and discipline. However, the evidence that uniforms improve academic outcomes is weak, and the savings are sometimes overstated, since schools often require specific items that are sold only by one supplier at high prices. Uniforms can also restrict self expression, which is part of how teenagers develop identity. A reasonable compromise is a dress code that sets clear limits on clothing that is unsafe or disruptive, while leaving students free to choose within those limits. This keeps the goals of uniforms, such as focus and fairness, without forcing every child into the same identical clothes.

Artificial intelligence tools can now write essays, solve equations, and explain historical events in plain language, and schools have to decide how students should use them. Some educators want to ban these tools entirely, but a ban is hard to enforce and ignores the fact that AI will be part of most jobs students enter. A better approach is to teach students how to use AI as a support rather than a substitute. A tutor that asks guiding questions can help a student who is stuck on a proof, and a writing assistant can give feedback on structure while the student does the thinking. The risk is that students will rely on the tool to produce finished work and learn nothing. Teachers can reduce that risk by changing assignments, asking for drafts, requiring in-class discussion, and grading the process as well as the final product. The goal should not be to catch cheating but to make sure that students still build the skills the tools cannot provide for them.

Cities that want to reduce traffic and emissions should invest in public transit, and they should do it before congestion becomes unbearable. Buses and trains move far more people per lane than cars, which means that a single transit line can replace thousands of vehicles on crowded roads. Transit also gives people who cannot drive, including older residents and teenagers, a way to reach jobs and services. Opponents often point to low ridership on some systems and high operating costs, and both problems are real. However, ridership depends on frequency and reliability. A bus that comes every 30 minutes will never attract the same riders as one that comes every ten. Dedicated bus lanes, timed signals, and simple fares can improve service without enormous capital spending. Funding transit is a choice about what kind of city people want to live in. A place that relies only on cars will keep paying for roads and parking, while a place with good transit gives its residents more options at lower long term cost.

In many countries, students are not allowed to use mobile phones during lessons, and I think this rule is good for students. The phone is very distracting. When a student has a phone on the desk, they will look at it many times in one lesson, even if they do not want to. Notifications from messaging apps and games take their attention away from the teacher. Some people say that phones are useful for research and for translation, so banning them is unfair. This is true, but schools can keep phones in lockers during class and still allow them at break time or for specific tasks with teacher permission. Also, students learn better when they write notes by hand and listen carefully. In my experience, the students who keep their phones in their bags do better in exams. Because of this, I think a complete ban in classrooms is the right decision for most schools, and the benefits for concentration are bigger than the small inconvenience of not having the phone.

Should the voting age be lowered to 16? Yes and no. Arguments for: sixteen year olds pay taxes in some places, work jobs, and can be tried as adults for serious crimes in several countries. If they are old enough for those things, why not for voting. Countries like Austria and Brazil already allow it in some form and have not collapsed. Arguments against: many 16 year olds are still in school and are less exposed to politics. Brain development in the areas of planning is not finished until the mid twenties, though this argument is contested. Also, parents may influence votes. Honestly I think the strongest point is about consistency. We already let adults make big decisions with long consequences, and voting is one of the few ways teens can have a say about their future, which is the thing they care about most. Lowering the age to 16 would not solve every problem with youth turnout, but it would build the habit of voting early, and that habit tends to last. So I support it, with civic education in schools to go with it.

ok so are video games actually bad for kids. my honest take is no, not by default. The 'games rot your brain' stuff is kind of overblown, and most studies show correlation at best. But games can definitely become a problem when they replace sleep or school or friends. I know people who played 12 hours a day and dropped out, and I also know people who got really good at problem solving and teamwork from games and are now engineers. The real difference is whether the kid has other stuff going on and whether the game is designed to keep them hooked, like loot boxes or daily login rewards. Parents should look at those features more than the rating on the box. Also games let kids hang out with friends after school when they cant go outside, which matters a lot for kids who are isolated. So I think the answer is balance and some limits, not a ban. Banning usually makes the games more exciting.

Last summer I worked at a grocery store for twelve weeks, and it changed how I think about the minimum wage debate. Before the job, I thought the minimum wage was just a number politicians argued about. Working the register, stocking shelves, and dealing with customers showed me how many adults depend on jobs like mine for their entire income. My coworker Maria had two kids and worked two shifts a week at another store as well. She was not lazy, she was just stuck. I do understand the economists who say that raising the minimum wage can cost some jobs, and I think the evidence on that is mixed. Still, when I see what full time work at the minimum pays, I find it hard to believe that the market alone will fix that. A modest increase, phased in gradually and adjusted for local living costs, seems like a reasonable middle ground to me.

Government should continue to spend money on space exploration. Some people think this money should go to hospitals, schools, and poor families instead, and I understand this feeling. But space programs also bring many benefits that are not always visible. For example, satellites help with weather forecasting, which saves lives during hurricanes, and GPS is used by farmers, pilots, and delivery companies every day. Space research also creates new technology, like improved materials and medical imaging, that later enters ordinary life. Moreover, a space program gives young people a reason to study science and engineering, and it encourages international cooperation even between countries that disagree on other things. The total cost is not as large as many think. In most countries, the space budget is less than one percent of government spending. Therefore, I believe that a country that can afford to invest in space should do so, because the knowledge and skills it creates will help future generations solve problems on Earth as well.

Four day school weeks. Good or bad? Some rural districts in the US moved to four day weeks to save money on transport and utilities, and a few report better attendance and teacher retention. That is a real benefit. Teachers can have more time for planning and families can schedule appointments on the fifth day. But the research is mixed. Some studies find small drops in math scores, especially for younger students. The longer school days can be tiring for kids, and the childcare problem falls on working parents. Low income students who depend on free school meals lose a day of food each week, which is a serious issue. So my position: four day weeks can work for some districts, especially where transport costs are very high, but they should only be adopted with a plan for childcare and meals. Simply cutting a day to save money without thinking about the students who need school the most is not a good trade. Districts should test it carefully and measure outcomes.

I used to think college athletes should not get paid because they're students, but after watching my roommate, who plays football, I've changed my mind. He's on the field maybe 30 hours a week for the team, he gets injured, and the school sells his jersey and makes millions off TV contracts. His scholarship covers tuition but not rent or food for the summer, and he says he sometimes can't afford the bus. The argument against pay is that it would wreck college sports, but the NCAA already lets players earn money from name and likeness deals now, which didn't destroy anything. So I think the real question is whether schools should share revenue directly. I'm not sure about the exact numbers, and the schools say the money goes to other sports too, but I think at least some direct payment makes sense, especially for the players who generate the most income.

Rent control is a policy that many cities adopt in response to rising housing costs, and it deserves a more careful debate than it usually gets. Supporters point out that tenants in rent stabilized apartments can stay in their homes for years, which protects families and older residents from being pushed out. Opponents argue that price caps reduce the incentive to build new housing and to maintain existing units. Economists across the political spectrum have documented these effects in studies of cities such as San Francisco and St Paul, although the magnitude of the supply effect depends on how the policy is designed. A strict cap that applies to all buildings, including new ones, is more likely to reduce construction. A policy that exempts new buildings for a number of years, and limits increases to a reasonable percentage above inflation, can protect current tenants while leaving room for developers. In my view, the best version of rent control is a narrow one, paired with aggressive zoning reform that makes it easier to build homes at every price level.

Public libraries are very important for communities, and they should receive more funding from the local government. Many people think libraries are only for books, but today they offer much more. In my town, the library has free internet for people who do not have it at home, and job seekers use the computers to write their resumes. It also has classes for elderly people who are learning to use smartphones, and children's reading programs that help kids improve their language skills before they go to school. These services are especially important for poor families, who cannot pay for private tutors or expensive courses. Some argue that the money could be better spent on roads or police, but libraries are cheap compared with other services, and they reduce costs in other areas by helping people find work and learn new skills. For this reason, I think the city council should increase the library budget, and should consider opening more branches in neighborhoods where people have less access.

In my country, a wedding is not a single day for the couple. It is a project for the whole family. My aunt started cooking for the wedding six weeks before. My uncle rented the hall, which he did not like, but he says it is his duty. When I told my American coworkers this, they thought it was stressful. Maybe it is. But also nobody is alone. When my brother got married here in Texas, only twelve people came and everyone was polite and quiet. I missed the noise. I missed my cousins arguing about the music. I think a wedding should be a little bit too much, so people remember it and so the young couple feels they are not starting alone.

My cat has now claimed the one chair I bought for the home office. The chair was expensive. The chair had lumbar support and a five year warranty. The cat has no interest in lumbar support. Our HPA kept flapping between 4 and 11 replicas every few minutes and it took us most of a Friday to see why. The custom metric was a queue depth exported by a sidecar, scraped every 15s, but the adapter was averaging over a 30s window, so we were scaling on stale data that oscillated with the consumer lag. Classic. We added a stabilizationWindowSeconds of 300 on scale down and pinned the averageValue target against the actual drain rate instead of raw depth. The thing I didn't expect: the flapping was amplifying itself because new pods took 40s to pass readiness and the metric lagged behind them. Lesson: if your autoscaler is hunting, check your scrape interval before you touch the algorithm.

Nights are weird. You stop feeling like a person by about 3am. The hallway lights hum. Somebody's call bell goes off in room 12 and you know, without looking, it's the guy who just wants water and company. You bring the water. You sit for four minutes. Those four minutes are the part nobody puts in the staffing spreadsheet, and they're the part I think about when I drive home at 8 in the morning with the sun coming up over the parking garage. I'm not writing this to be inspiring. I'm writing it because my sister asked what I actually do all night, and I didn't have a good answer until I wrote it down.
tactic: very short sentences mixed with long ones

text: Been running this plumbing shop for nineteen years, two trucks, one part-time guy named Ray who knows more about water heaters than anyone in the county. People ask me why I don't do the flashy stuff, like smart leak sensors and app-controlled everything. Simple. The flashy stuff breaks, and then someone calls me at 9pm on a Sunday. I'd rather fix a boring cast-iron drain right the first time. Last month a lady in Maple Heights had a water heater with a corroded anode rod. She'd been told it needed replacing for three years by a guy who wanted to sell her a whole new unit. We pulled the rod, it was basically gone, and we put a new one in for a hundred and forty bucks. That's what I'm proud of.

Every spring the city council discusses protected bike lanes, and every spring the same argument plays out: the lanes take parking, and parking matters to downtown businesses. It is a fair concern on paper. But when the city painted a two-block stretch of Carver Avenue last year, the coffee shop on the corner reported more morning customers, not fewer. The reason was boring. Cyclists who felt safe stopped on their way in, and people who used to drive to the next town started walking past storefronts. Counts from the traffic department show roughly 40 percent more cycling trips on that stretch, though those numbers come from a single summer and should be treated carefully. Still, the parking argument deserves a second look before it wins again.
tactic: measured, hedged civic argument in a blog

text: I'm a nurse who learned SQL at 2am during night shifts, and six months ago I got my first analyst offer. People ask how I did it. The honest answer is boring. I did a free course, then I built a dashboard tracking fall incidents on my own unit using de-identified data we were already reporting, and I brought it to my nurse manager. She cried a little. Then she asked me to present it at committee. That presentation got me the interview. Nobody in the hiring panel cared about my certificate. They cared that I understood what a fall-risk score actually means at the bedside. If you're switching careers, don't try to become a generic analyst. Bring the thing you already know that other people don't.

I started learning guitar at 40 because a guy at my office brought one to the holiday party and played Wonderwall badly and everyone sang anyway. It stuck with me. Eight months later I can play about nine songs and a rough version of a blues shuffle that my neighbor says sounds like a dog falling down stairs. Adult learners get weird advice. Some people say you can't get good after 30. That's nonsense. You just have to accept that your fingers will hurt for three weeks and that you will sound terrible in front of your kids. My practice is twenty minutes a day, mostly chord changes, with a metronome set to 60 that I keep forgetting to turn up. The progress is slow. It's also the most fun I've had in years.

I made a hiring mistake last year that cost us about four months and one very good engineer who left. I hired for the interview. The candidate was sharp, fast, and gave beautiful answers about system design. What I didn't check was how they handled being wrong in a room. On the job, they dug in on a bad architectural decision for six weeks and wouldn't let anyone else touch the service. Now my interview loop includes a deliberate pushback exercise. I give a flawed design and watch what happens when they're told it's flawed. Some candidates get defensive, some get curious. Curious wins every time. We've hired three people since with this loop and none of them have been a problem.

text: People think making pottery is about clay. It's mostly about water and patience. Last winter I threw eighteen bowls in a row and every single one collapsed at the rim because my wheel speed was too high and I was rushing the pull. I wanted to quit. Instead I threw them again, slower, and kept a sponge within reach like a nervous parent. The studio where I rent time has an old Brent wheel that screams when you push it past its limit, which is honestly a useful teacher. Glazing is a whole other universe. I still can't predict how a celadon will break on a bowl, and I've stopped trying. Some pieces come out of the kiln looking like a stranger's work. I've started to like that.

My conference talk got rejected. Again. Third year in a row. The email was polite and said 'we received an unusually high number of submissions' which I've learned is code for 'we didn't pick you.' So I rewrote it around the mistakes, submitted to a smaller regional event, and got accepted. If your talk got rejected, the problem is probably the framing, not the content.

text: Late blight came through our county in July, which is earlier than I've seen in eleven years of growing tomatoes out here near Wooster. The first sign was a brown patch on the lower leaves of the Cherokee Purples, then the stems turned black and by the weekend half the bed looked like it had been rained on with ash. I pulled everything I could. I did not compost the infected plants, which I know is the thing everyone says, but I bagged them and put them in the trash because my compost pile gets hot and I didn't want to gamble. The configuration loader reads settings from three sources, in order of increasing priority: a default file shipped with the package, a project-level file named config.yaml in the working directory, and environment variables prefixed with APP_. Values from later sources override earlier ones, so an environment variable always wins. Nested keys are flattened using double underscores, which means that APP_DATABASE__HOST maps to database.host in the YAML file. If a required key is missing after all three sources have been merged, the loader raises a ConfigError that lists every missing key at once, rather than failing on the first one. This makes it easier to fix a broken deployment in a single pass. To inspect the final merged configuration, call load_config(debug=True), which prints the resolved values with secrets masked.

If the build fails with a message about a missing native module, the most likely cause is a mismatch between the Node.js version used to install dependencies and the version used to run the application. Native modules are compiled against a specific ABI, so switching versions without reinstalling will break them. To resolve the problem, delete the node_modules directory and the lockfile cache, confirm the active version with node --version, and run the install command again. If you use a version manager, make sure the shell session that runs the build has loaded the same version as the one you used during installation. Continuous integration environments are a common source of this issue, because the cached dependency layer may have been created with an older runtime. Clearing the cache usually fixes it.

Version 2.4.0 introduces pagination support for the list endpoints. Previously, GET /v1/items returned every record in a single response, which caused timeouts for accounts with large datasets. The endpoint now accepts a limit parameter, with a default of 50 and a maximum of 200, and a cursor parameter that is returned in the next_cursor field of each response. When next_cursor is null, you have reached the final page. Clients that do not send either parameter will receive the first fifty items, which is a behavior change from earlier releases. We recommend updating any integration that assumed a complete result set. The older unpaginated behavior is available temporarily by sending the header X-Legacy-Pagination: true, but this header will be removed in version 3.0.0.

You can fix this by wrapping the call in a try/finally block so that the connection is always released back to the pool. The problem you are seeing happens because the exception is raised before conn.close() runs, which leaves the connection checked out. Over time the pool runs out of available connections, and new requests block until the timeout expires. A cleaner approach is to use the connection as a context manager, since the with statement guarantees that cleanup runs even when an error occurs. Also consider lowering the pool timeout so that a leak shows up as an error quickly instead of as a slow, mysterious hang. Finally, enable logging for the pool so you can see how many connections are in use at any moment.

To get started, clone the repository and install the dependencies with your package manager of choice. Copy the example environment file to .env and fill in the required values, including the database URL and the secret used for signing tokens. Run the migration command to create the tables, then start the development server. The application will be available on port 3000 by default, and it reloads automatically when you change a source file. To run the test suite, use the test script defined in package.json. Tests use an in-memory database, so they do not require any additional setup. If you want to contribute, please read the contributing guide first, and open an issue to discuss any large change before submitting a pull request.

The retry middleware wraps outgoing HTTP calls and repeats them when the response indicates a transient failure. By default it retries on status codes 502, 503, and 504, as well as on connection resets, up to three times. Delays between attempts grow exponentially, starting at 200 milliseconds, and a small random jitter is added to avoid synchronized retries from many clients. Requests that are not idempotent, such as POST, are not retried unless you explicitly set retry_unsafe to true. When all attempts fail, the middleware raises the last error it received, and the number of attempts is attached to the exception so it can be logged. You can customize the policy by passing a RetryPolicy object when creating the client.

This page describes how on-call handoff works for the platform team. At the start of each rotation, the outgoing engineer writes a summary of open incidents, flaky alerts, and any ongoing maintenance in the handoff document. The incoming engineer reads it before the handoff meeting, which is held on Monday at ten in the morning, and asks questions about anything unclear. During the rotation, the on-call engineer is expected to acknowledge pages within five minutes and to post updates in the incident channel at regular intervals. If an issue cannot be resolved within an hour, escalate to the secondary on-call. After a rotation ends, any alert that fired more than three times should be reviewed and either fixed or tuned.

The cache layer stores computed results keyed by a hash of the input arguments. Each entry has a time-to-live, set to ten minutes unless you override it, after which the entry is treated as missing and is recomputed on the next call. The cache is process-local, so each worker maintains its own copy, and entries are not shared across instances. If you need shared state, configure the Redis backend instead, which uses the same interface. To invalidate a single entry, call cache.delete with the same arguments that were used to create it. To clear everything, call cache.clear. Be careful when caching functions that depend on global state, because the cache key only includes the arguments you pass explicitly.

Authentication in the API uses bearer tokens, which you obtain by sending your client credentials to the token endpoint. Each token is valid for one hour, and the response includes an expires_in field so that your client can refresh it before it lapses. Include the token in the Authorization header of every request, using the format Bearer followed by the token. If a request is made with an expired or malformed token, the server responds with status 401 and a JSON body describing the reason. Do not store tokens in client-side code or in version control. For server-to-server integrations, we recommend requesting a new token on startup and caching it in memory until shortly before it expires.

A common cause of slow queries in this service is a missing index on the tenant_id column. Because almost every query filters by tenant, the database performs a full table scan when no index exists, and the cost grows with the size of the table. To confirm, run EXPLAIN on the slow query and look for a sequential scan. Adding a composite index on tenant_id and created_at usually resolves the problem for list views that sort by date. Create the index concurrently on production systems to avoid locking writes. After the index is built, run ANALYZE so that the planner has up-to-date statistics, and compare the query time before and after the change.

The scheduler runs jobs on a fixed cron-style schedule and guarantees that no two instances of the same job run at the same time. It achieves this with a lock stored in the database, which is renewed periodically while the job is running. If a worker crashes, the lock expires after sixty seconds and another worker can pick the job up. Jobs should therefore be written to be safe to run more than once, because a crash during execution may lead to a repeat. Job status, start time, and duration are recorded in the jobs table, and failures are reported to the alerting channel after the second consecutive error.

Environment variables control most of the runtime behavior of the container image. LOG_LEVEL sets the verbosity and accepts debug, info, warn, or error. PORT sets the listening port and defaults to 8080. DATABASE_URL is required and must be a valid connection string. When running in Kubernetes, provide sensitive values through secrets rather than through plain environment entries in the manifest. The image runs as a non-root user and expects a writable temporary directory, so if you mount the root filesystem as read-only, add an empty volume at the temp path. Health checks are exposed at the /healthz endpoint, which returns status 200 when the application is ready to serve traffic.

Question: why does my React component re-render on every keystroke? Answer: the most common reason is that you are creating a new object or function on each render and passing it as a prop to a memoized child. Because the reference changes every time, the shallow comparison fails and the child updates. Wrap the function in useCallback and the object in useMemo, with the correct dependency arrays, and the child will only render when the underlying values change. Another possible cause is that the state lives too high in the tree, so a keystroke in one input updates a parent that renders many unrelated children. Moving the state down into the input component, or using an uncontrolled input, often removes the problem entirely.

Release process: tag the commit on main using semantic versioning, for example v1.4.0, and push the tag. The release pipeline then builds the artifacts, runs the full test suite, and publishes the package to the registry. While the pipeline runs, update the changelog with a short summary of user-visible changes, grouped by fixes, features, and breaking changes. Once the pipeline succeeds, create the release entry on the hosting platform and link the changelog. If the pipeline fails after publishing partially, do not re-tag; instead, fix the issue and cut a patch release. Announce the release in the engineering channel with a link to the notes.

text: How to rotate the signing key, short version. 1) generate new key pair, dont delete the old one. 2) add new public key to the JWKS endpoint config, deploy. 3) wait at least 24h, tokens are valid 12h so old ones should be gone by then. 4) switch the signer to the new private key, deploy. 5) remove the old public key after another day. text: Social media has made it easier than ever to stay connected, yet many people report feeling more isolated than before. This apparent contradiction deserves careful attention. On one hand, platforms allow families separated by oceans to share daily moments, and they give people with niche interests a place to find others who share them. On the other hand, constant exposure to curated images of other people's lives can encourage unhealthy comparison, and time spent scrolling often replaces time spent in person. In my view, the technology itself is neither good nor bad; the outcome depends on how it is used. Individuals should set limits on their own usage, and schools should teach students how to evaluate what they see online. A balanced approach will let society enjoy the benefits while limiting the harm.

Should university education be free for everyone? Supporters argue that access to higher education is a basic right and that removing tuition would reduce inequality. They point out that countries such as Germany have abolished fees without damaging the quality of their universities. Critics respond that free tuition is expensive, and that the cost would fall on taxpayers, many of whom never attend university. There is also a concern that without any financial stake, students may be less committed to their studies. After weighing both sides, I believe that tuition should be heavily subsidized but not entirely eliminated. A system of grants for low-income students, combined with modest fees for others, would widen access while keeping the system sustainable.

Homework has long been a standard part of school life, but its value is increasingly questioned. Proponents claim that it reinforces what students learn in class and teaches responsibility and time management. However, research suggests that the benefits are small for younger children, and excessive homework can cause stress and reduce time for sleep, play, and family. For this reason, I argue that schools should limit homework, especially in primary grades, and focus on quality rather than quantity. Short, meaningful tasks that encourage curiosity are more useful than hours of repetitive exercises. Teachers should also coordinate with one another so that students are not overloaded on a single night. In conclusion, homework should support learning, not dominate childhood.

Remote work has changed how people think about the office. During the pandemic, millions of employees discovered that many tasks could be done from home, and many of them now prefer to continue. Working remotely saves commuting time, reduces costs, and can improve the balance between work and personal life. Nevertheless, it also has drawbacks, including weaker team bonds, difficulty separating work from home, and fewer chances for junior staff to learn from colleagues. I think the best solution is a hybrid model, in which employees spend a few days in the office and the rest at home. This arrangement keeps the social and mentoring benefits of the workplace while preserving flexibility. Companies that adopt it thoughtfully are likely to attract and keep talented workers.

Is it ethical to use animals in medical research? This question divides opinion sharply. Those in favor argue that animal studies have led to vaccines, surgical techniques, and treatments that have saved millions of lives, and that there is often no adequate substitute. Opponents counter that animals can suffer and that humans have no right to cause them pain for their own benefit. While I respect both positions, I believe that animal research can be justified only under strict conditions. Researchers should use animals only when no alternative exists, use as few as possible, and minimize suffering. Investment in computer models and cell cultures should also continue, so that the need for animal testing declines over time.

Many cities are struggling with traffic congestion, and one proposed solution is to make public transport free. The idea has clear advantages. It would encourage more people to leave their cars at home, reduce pollution, and help low-income residents who cannot afford fares. However, the policy would also remove a major source of income for transit agencies, and without extra funding service quality might suffer. In addition, some studies indicate that free fares attract mainly people who would otherwise walk or cycle, rather than drivers. I therefore conclude that free transport alone is not enough. Cities should combine better service, lower fares, and measures such as congestion charges to discourage driving effectively.

The rise of artificial intelligence raises the question of whether machines will take over human jobs. History offers some guidance. Earlier technologies, from the steam engine to the computer, destroyed certain occupations but created new ones, and living standards rose overall. Yet the transition was painful for those who lost their work, and there is no guarantee that the pattern will repeat. AI is different because it can perform cognitive tasks, not only physical ones. In my opinion, governments should prepare by investing in retraining programs and by strengthening the social safety net. Workers who can adapt will be able to benefit, but society must make sure that no one is left behind.

Some people believe that zoos should be abolished because keeping animals in captivity is cruel. Others say that zoos protect endangered species and educate the public. Both views contain some truth. Modern zoos often take part in breeding programs that have saved species such as the Arabian oryx from extinction, and many visitors develop an interest in conservation after seeing animals up close. At the same time, small enclosures can harm large, intelligent animals like elephants and orcas. My position is that zoos should be judged by their standards. Those that provide spacious habitats and support real conservation work should be allowed to continue, while poor facilities should be closed.

Online learning is often presented as the future of education. It offers flexibility, lower costs, and access to teachers from around the world. Students who live in remote areas can study courses that were once available only in big cities. Still, online learning requires strong self-discipline, and many learners drop out because they feel isolated or lack support. Younger children in particular benefit from face-to-face contact with teachers and classmates. I believe that online courses are an excellent supplement but not a full replacement for traditional schools. The best results come from blending the two, using technology to extend what teachers can do rather than to replace them.

Is fast fashion a serious problem? Cheap clothing allows many people to follow trends without spending much, but this convenience carries a hidden price. Garment factories often pay low wages and have unsafe conditions, and the industry produces large amounts of waste and carbon emissions. Discarded clothes fill landfills within months of being bought. Consumers can make a difference by buying fewer, better items and by choosing secondhand options. Governments also have a role, for example by requiring companies to report on their supply chains. In conclusion, fast fashion is a problem that demands action from both shoppers and lawmakers, because low prices should not come at the expense of people and the planet.

I think relationships and free time matters more once your basic needs are covered. So money helps, but its not the main thing.

What actually worked for my team was dumb and small. We pick ONE thing. Just one. Somebody owns it with a name next to it and a date. Next retro we open with that one thing before anything else and ask: did it happen, yes or no.

That's the whole trick. Accountability for one item beats a wall of fifteen good intentions.

Will this work for everyone? No idea. Bigger orgs probably need more structure. But for teams under ten I'd bet money on it. Fight me in the comments.

Today I want talk about something what many founders in my country are not saying loudly: hiring first employee is more scary than raising money.

When I hired my first developer in Pune, I did not sleep for three nights. Money is only number. But person has family, has rent, has expectations. If my business fail, it is not only my failure.

Spent six hours yesterday chasing a bug where our Postgres connection pool kept exhausting under load, only in staging, never locally. Classic.

Turned out a background job was opening a transaction, calling an external API with a 30s timeout, and only then committing. So under a slow vendor, every worker held a connection hostage. PgBouncer in transaction mode didn't help because the transaction was literally open the whole time.

Fix: move the HTTP call outside the transaction boundary, write an outbox row inside it, let a separate poller do the network bit. Idle-in-transaction count went from 40ish to basically zero.

Lesson I keep relearning: never do I/O you don't control while holding a lock or a connection. Ever. Put it in the checklist, tattoo it on your forearm, whatever works.

My dad was a welder for 34 years and he never once called what he did a craft. He said it was a job. But I watched him, as a kid, spend an entire Saturday regrinding a bead because it didn't look right to him even though nobody would ever see it. It was inside a flange.

I think about that a lot now that I manage people. Everybody wants culture decks and values workshops. Meanwhile the thing that actually matters is whether someone will redo a thing nobody checks.

You can't really train that. You can hire for it, a bit, by asking people about the last time they fixed something no one noticed. The good ones light up. The others give you a rehearsed answer about stakeholder alignment.

Anyway. Miss him. Call your folks.

Language choice is maybe 5 percent of the outcome. Finishing things is the other 95. Not scientific, I just made that number up, but you know it's close.

Hot take about remote work, and I'm gonna get yelled at: the problem was never location. It's meetings that should've been a paragraph.

We went fully remote in 2020, then back to hybrid in 2023, and productivity barely moved either direction. What moved was how many calendar invites I got. Went from 11 a week to 29. Twenty-nine! Half of them had no agenda.

So I started declining anything without an agenda. Politely, with a note. First week people were annoyed. By week three, three colleagues copied me and now our team has about 14 meetings a week and we ship faster.

Anyway. Not a return-to-office argument or a stay-home argument. Just: write the agenda or cancel the call.

I moved here eight months ago from Lagos for a data engineering role. The job is great. The paperwork nearly broke me. I cried once in a Albert Heijn over a bag of sugar, don't ask.

If you're new somewhere, find one person. Just one.

I reviewed 40 pull requests this week. Here is what I flagged most. Not clever stuff. Boring stuff.

Naming. A function called handleData that does five things. Error handling that logs and moves on. A try/catch wrapped around the entire file. Comments that restate the code, like '// increment i'. Tests that assert the mock was called, and nothing else.

None of this is hard to fix. It just needs somebody to care for ten extra minutes before hitting submit. Junior or senior, makes no difference. I've seen staff engineers ship a function named doStuff.

If you want to level up fast, read your own diff top to bottom before you ask anyone else to. You'll catch half of it yourself.

text:
I've been a hiring manager for nine years and I'll tell you what I wish candidates knew. The cover letter doesn't matter much. The resume matters a bit. What matters is whether you can tell me about one thing you screwed up without getting weird about it.

There's a certain flavour of answer. 'My biggest weakness is that I care too much.' No. Stop. I've heard it four hundred times and I stopped hearing it around number twelve.

Tell me about the migration you broke on a Friday. Tell me about the client you mis-quoted. I'll lean forward. Real mistakes, small and specific, with what you changed after, make me trust you immediately.

Honestly I'd rather hire someone who's failed visibly than someone who's never been tested.

My grandmother's garden in Kerala had one jackfruit tree that fed half the street. She never sold a single fruit. When I asked why, she said, 'If you sell it, you have to count it. If you give it, you only have to remember who was hungry.'

I've been thinking about that sentence while running our little co-op. We are twelve women making coconut oil soap. Last month a supplier raised prices by 18 percent and everyone panicked about margins. But then Sheela suggested we simply tell customers the truth, that costs went up, and ask if they'd stay with us. Ninety percent stayed. Some even paid extra.

People aren't always cold about money. Sometimes they just want to be told honestly.

TIL that the 'five whys' technique falls apart if you stop at five. We had an outage last quarter. Why did the service go down? Memory. Why memory? A leak. Why a leak? An unclosed stream. Why unclosed? A missing finally block. Why missing? Developer forgot.

Great. Blame the dev. Except if you keep going, why did nobody catch it? No linter rule. Why no rule? Nobody owned the lint config. Why? We reorganized in March and the platform team lost two people.

The real cause wasn't a missing finally block. It was a staffing decision made in March. You only see it if you refuse to stop at the first human.

I now ask 'why' until it stops being about a person and starts being about a process.

A short note on pricing for freelancers, because I see this mistake constantly.

You are not charging for hours. You are charging for the problem going away. If a logo takes me two hours but the client then lands a 40k contract because of it, the logo is not a two hour product. Stop dividing your rate by the clock.

I used to charge 35 an hour. Barely scraped by. Switched to fixed project fees in 2021 and my income roughly doubled without me working more. Some clients balked, and honestly, good riddance, those were the ones who haggled over invoices and paid at day 60.

Start small. Pick one project, quote a flat fee, see what happens. Worst case, you learn something.
